en: A global tidal-energy atlas is a secondary source for spotting where the difference is large; local studies then check whether that spot can actually be built.
The competency asks for situations where the tidal difference could be exploited, meaning converted to useful electricity, not merely watched from a pier.
Sources group sites into closed-basin barrages or lagoons versus open-stream turbines, two different situations for using the same tidal rise and fall.
Unlike solar power, a tidal difference still arrives at night, a reason secondary energy comparisons list tides as a complementary renewable.
If a paper says a mean range of about five meters, copy it as 'about five meters' and name the paper; do not invent a more dramatic number.
A complete identification names a site type that is both physically suitable and discussed as acceptable in the sources, not only a huge tide on a map.
To discuss a shower's regular timing, check a current astronomy almanac or PAGASA skywatch page rather than a random social-media date.
A shower is named for the constellation that holds its radiant, and that name stays the same year after year as the stream is crossed again.
Many annual showers come from a parent comet whose orbit still sheds dust, so Earth meets that dust on a schedule set by both orbits.
The Geminids are a regular December shower whose parent is an asteroid-like body, showing that not every annual stream is from a classic comet.
The Quadrantid meteor shower is a regular early-January event, another calendar marker listed in yearly meteor-shower tables.
A shower has a peak night and a wider season; reliable tables list both, so 'regular' does not mean only a single hour each year.
Random sporadic meteors can appear any night, but a shower is the regular, clustered burst when Earth hits a known dust stream.
Earth's year-long trip around the Sun is the clock: the same stretch of orbit is where a given shower's dust is waiting each year.
The shower still occurs on schedule even if a bright Moon hides many meteors, so regularity is about the stream, not about how many you personally see.
The Lyrids are a regular April shower tied to comet Thatcher, listed on annual sky calendars along with the better-known Perseids.
The Orionids return each October from dust of comet Halley, a regular shower whose parent comet is famous from other years as well.
The Eta Aquariids are a regular May shower also linked to comet Halley, showing one comet trail can make more than one annual meeting.
Many annual showers are visible from the Philippines, though some northern radiants sit lower; a local astronomy club table is a useful source.
A meteor storm is a rare extra-dense year, not the usual regular shower; textbooks separate those outliers from the ordinary annual return.
When you copy a peak date, write the year of the table, because leap years and orbital drift can shift the listed night by a day.
Some streams are centuries old, yet Earth still crosses them on a yearly rhythm, which is why the shower is called regular even if the comet is faint now.
The meteors do not come from the stars of Perseus or Gemini; those names only mark the sky direction of a regular, nearby dust crossing.
Many annual showers are better after midnight because that side of Earth then faces into the dust stream, a regular geometric reason in the sources.
The Ursids are a quieter regular shower near late December, often listed beside the Geminids on the same yearly meteor calendar.
How many nights a shower lasts depends on how wide the dust stream is, which is why some regular showers are short and others last weeks.
Yearly tables also list typical meteor speed for each shower, another regular property of that stream, not a new surprise each August.
Photographers plan the same showers on the same weeks each year, practical evidence that the occurrence is regular enough to schedule.
Secondary sources group mutations as beneficial, harmful, or neutral depending on whether they help, hurt, or barely change an organism's survival.
A well-studied beneficial mutation lets some adults keep digesting milk sugar, an example textbooks cite from human population genetics.
